extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, publishers, and readers interested in publication integrity
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and evaluating signs of fraudulent authorship, unverifiable affiliations, and citation manipulation in journal submissions and published papers, and the editorial policies and actions relevant to those problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifiable affiliations / existence of claimed employers
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction notices cited that “the existence and nature” of a company couldn’t be confirmed; many claimed companies do not appear in business registries and have no verifiable online presence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check corporate listings, domain registrations, archived website snapshots, and contact information. A claimed employer should be locatable in public registries or via legitimate online presence; inability to do so is a red flag for affiliation falsification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship changes before acceptance require editor approval and written explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: According to a December 2024 guide, any changes to authorship before a paper is accepted should be approved by the editor and accompanied by a written explanation; authors are “now required” to submit a form for editorial consideration to change authorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should enforce a policy requiring documented rationale and formal forms for any authorship change during revision, and record when the requirement began. Lack of proper approval/documentation should block or trigger investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sudden addition of multiple authors during revision as a paper-mill indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Pattern observed: a solo author submits a paper claiming an affiliation with an unverified company; during revision the author adds several other authors — including new first and corresponding authors — despite no clear contribution to the original work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat sudden authorship additions (especially adding first/corresponding authors) without clear contribution statements as strong indicators of paper mills or authorship-for-sale schemes; investigate provenance and contributions before acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors must be able to explain and justify authorship changes
rubrics_metrics.description: When editors asked, original authors were unable to explain why they added additional authors, nor validate the 'nature' or 'existence' of the companies they claimed affiliation with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require submitting authors to provide a clear, plausible explanation for any authorship changes and supporting evidence; inability or refusal to explain should prompt rejection, correction, or retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized authorship changes during review should prompt investigation and can affect published papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Elsevier discovered 'unauthorized authorship changes' during the review process, which prompted a wider investigation; many issues were found in papers already published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers and editors must monitor for and investigate unauthorized changes in authorship at all stages (submission, revision, production), and be prepared to investigate and, if necessary, retract published articles where unauthorized changes are discovered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corresponding authors must be contactable and responsive
rubrics_metrics.description: Nearly all of the newly added corresponding authors did not respond to requests for comment; one submitting author who had a listed email did not respond to requests for proof of affiliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require reliable contact information for corresponding authors and confirm responsiveness during review; uncontactable corresponding authors are a red flag that merits further verification before publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting coordinated patterns across papers as evidence of fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Dozens of papers appear to follow an identical pattern of submission, affiliation claims, and authorship changes across multiple journals, indicating coordinated activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cluster analysis and pattern detection (similar affiliations, repeated submission behaviors, identical authorship-change patterns) across submissions/journals are useful tools for spotting coordinated paper-mill activity and should trigger broader investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspicious citation patterns / manufactured citations
rubrics_metrics.description: PubPeer commenters mentioned possibly manufactured citations; many of the retracted papers cite the same author repeatedly, and that cited author denied knowledge of the citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for anomalous citation concentrations (many papers repeatedly citing the same person/institute) and citations that appear unrelated to the content; such patterns may signal citation-inflation schemes and merit scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher workflow vulnerabilities enable exploitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters noted production-stage pages (e.g., a page asking if there were author changes with a + button) can allow author changes after review, potentially past the point an editor would see them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review and harden editorial and production workflows to prevent unauthorized or late-stage alterations to authorship; add checkpoints where editors must explicitly approve author changes before they are applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Falsified affiliations undermine trust in the research and can justify retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: If authors lie about their affiliations, it is unreasonable to trust their statements about experiments or results, and the paper may be of no scientific value; sudden additions of authorship are often flags that the paper was written by someone else and offered for sale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider falsified provenance (affiliations/authorship) as undermining the integrity of reported research; such findings justify corrections or retractions even if the paper's content appears sound, because provenance affects trustworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction grounds: unauthorized authorship changes and unverifiable affiliations
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction notices attributed decisions to suspicious changes in authorship and the authors being unable to verify the existence of their employers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers may legitimately retract articles when authorship changes are unauthorized or when affiliations/employers cannot be verified, especially where such issues indicate potential fraud or fabricated provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial responsibility to follow up on external sleuthing and request evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: An independent researcher flagged papers and provided commentary on PubPeer; the publisher asked him for evidence that a company was fake and conducted its own investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and publishers should take credible external reports (PubPeer, sleuthing) seriously, request/assess evidence, and perform due diligence investigations rather than dismissing outside alerts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affiliation claims should correspond to legitimate registry/online presence
rubrics_metrics.description: Claimed companies (e.g., 'Sun-life', 'Arian company') were absent from national registries or were businesses in unrelated industries; domains were transient or irrelevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify that claimed institutional affiliations correspond to appropriate registry entries or legitimate organizational information (location, industry, contact details); mismatches or unrelated business types are suspicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship-for-sale signature: repeated submitting authors vs one-off added authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Original submitting authors published several papers each, while the authors added during revision often appear only once among the retracted papers — a pattern suggesting authorship-for-sale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag submission sets where a small set of submitters repeatedly publish many papers while added coauthors appear only once; this asymmetry can indicate fraudulent resale of authorship rather than genuine collaboration.
